commands.speak: Now that we have seen what the QALY can and cannot see, here are its rivals, side by side.
The QALY counts health gained, weighted by preferences — comparable across any disease, but health only.
The DALY, the disability-adjusted life year, turns it around: it counts health lost, years of life lost plus years lived with disability.
Its disability weights run the other way, 0 for full health and 1 for death, and they underpin the Global Burden of Disease studies.
Its strength is one yardstick for every country; its weakness is that the weights judge health, not what people would give up for it.
The WELLBY counts life satisfaction: one point on a 0 to 10 scale, for one person, for one year.
It reaches beyond health, so a housing policy and a drug can be compared; Britain's Treasury has guidance for using it.
But it counts adaptation in full — the very issue we began with.
Capability measures such as ICECAP-O, for older people, ask what a person is able to do and be: attachment, security, role, enjoyment, control.
They value freedom rather than function, but there is no settled way yet to weigh them against years of life.
Each rival repairs one blind spot and opens another.
So a cost per QALY is not a fact about a drug: it carries a choice of whose values, which method, and which questionnaire.
Its strength is that those choices are written down, so they can be checked, changed and argued over in the open.
Read any ICER with those three questions, and you can see what the number measures — and what it leaves out.

quiz.question: Two analyses of the same drug report 18,000 and 35,000 per QALY. Before calling one of them wrong, what should you check first?
choices: Whose values, which method, which questionnaire
quiz.right: The three choices behind the weights: whose values, which method, which questionnaire can each move an ICER that far.
quiz.wrong: Think back over what moved our example's ICER in this lecture.
